content.title: About
content.content: Avocado is the fruit of the avocado tree (Persea americana) native to tropical and subtropical regions. The fruit has a creamy, slightly nutty flesh rich in healthy fats and is commonly used in sandwiches, salads, and smoothies.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Avocado is often called the "butter fruit" because of its high monounsaturated fat content.
The world’s largest avocado weighed over 5 kg.
The pit contains about 20 % oil, which is used in cosmetics.
There are more than 500 avocado varieties, with Hass and Fuerte being the most popular.
Avocado contains no sugar but has a natural mild sweetness.

items.title: Rich in monounsaturated fats
items.content: These fats help lower LDL cholesterol and support heart health.

items.title: Source of vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K is essential for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Contains potassium
items.content: Potassium aids in blood pressure regulation and muscle function.

items.title: Folate
items.content: Folate is important for cell division and especially vital during pregnancy.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber improves digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to avocado, particularly those with latex allergy.

items.title: High calorie density
items.content: Avocado is calorie‑dense, so portion control is advisable for weight‑management diets.

items.title: Possible drug interactions
items.content: Its high potassium content can affect certain medications, such as diuretics.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Slice avocado for sandwiches, mash it into a spread, add it to salads, or use it as a mayo substitute.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep whole avocados at room temperature until ripe, then refrigerate for up to 5 days. Store cut pieces in an airtight container with lemon juice to prevent browning.
